items.prompt: A muesli producer in Windhoek is deciding whether to spend its savings on developing a new pouched cereal range. Explain why developing new products matters to a business, and why the decision still carries risk.
items.canonical_answer: Developing new products matters because a fresh product gives customers a new reason to buy: tastes and fashions move, and a range that stands still loses attention, so the new pouches can refresh the producer's shelf presence and set it apart from rivals whose buyers then have a reason to switch. The reason development matters is that demand for newness exists. The risk sits beside it: the development costs - ingredients, testing, packaging and launch promotion - are paid before any revenue arrives, and the demand for a new product is unproven, so if customers do not want pouches the money spent is not recovered.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for why development matters - tastes move and a static range loses attention, so a new product refreshes the range and differentiates the business. Second reason: award for the risk side - costs are paid before revenue and demand is unproven, because a failed product means money not recovered.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the limitations a business faces when it develops a new product.
items.canonical_answer: The limitations have three features. First, up-front cost: ingredients, testing, redesigns and launch promotion are paid before the first sale, so the money leaves before any return is known. Second, unproven demand: until customers vote with their wallets the business cannot be sure they want the product at all - this is what it includes that a planned sales forecast is not. Third, failure risk: a product that fails leaves the development money spent with nothing coming back, and the parts of that risk - the launch promotion and the redesigns - are all sunk before the market answers.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - costs paid before revenue, demand unproven, failure means money not recovered - and one mark for what the limitation includes with an example such as launch promotion being sunk cost.

items.prompt: A Windhoegro bakery has spent five years keeping every batch consistent and now finds customers re-choose its name even when a rival undercuts its price. Explain how a trusted brand image leads from recognition to this loyalty, and what the bakery had to pay to get there.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: where the business has kept quality consistent for years, recognition builds. Mechanism: a known name lowers the risk a buyer feels at the moment of choice, so the buyer takes the comfortable option; a satisfied buyer then re-chooses the name that satisfied them, and loyal buyers weigh quality and habit against small price gaps rather than chasing each cheaper rival. Consequence for the business: sales hold up and the profit objective is served by customers who cost nothing extra to keep - which is the loyalty described. What it cost: consistent quality, promotion and packaging over years, and the stakeholder risk that one bad batch shared widely can damage in days what took years to build, so the image is an asset that must be maintained.

Mechanism: award for the why or how - a known name lowers felt risk, so purchases come easily and repeat. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - loyalty that holds sales and serves profit - and a second consequence for the cost side: the years of spending and the damage a failure can do.

items.prompt: A product's life cycle curve shows sales climbing steeply for two years, then flattening at a high level for the last three. Explain what the shape of the curve means by comparing the two phases, and what the flattening tells the business.
items.canonical_answer: Comparison: the steep climb means the growth stage - awareness spreading, so sales rise quickly year on year; the flat high level against it means maturity - sales holding, because most customers willing to buy already have it and rivals crowd in. The meaning of the flattening is that the easy gains are over: the product is established, but so is the competition, so price pressure begins and the business must decide between accepting steady maturity sales and paying for an extension strategy to push decline away. Interpreting the curve is reading which of those two phases the product is in, because the decisions differ.
marking_guidance: Comparison: award for setting the steep climb against the flat level and naming growth and maturity. Meaning: award for interpreting the flattening - established but rival-crowded, so extension decisions follow.

Third, carry the same reading into the pricing decision: at introduction set the price high to skim or low to penetrate, while at maturity stand near the rivals' level, because buyers compare close substitutes there. items.prompt: Explain the boundary between price elastic demand and price inelastic demand, and the test that tells one from the other.
items.canonical_answer: The boundary is the buyer's alternatives. Demand is price elastic where close substitutes are easy to buy: the quantity demanded responds more strongly than the price change, because customers simply switch, whereas demand is price inelastic where the product is needed, rare or habitual: the quantity demanded responds less strongly, because customers keep buying through a rise. Both sides share the same test: ask what happens to quantity demanded against the size of the price change - a small rise losing a large share of sales marks elastic, the same rise losing few sales marks inelastic. items.prompt: A learner writes: "Ondjila Cycles is using price skimming on its new electric bike: it has priced the bike below the other bike shops so it can skim their customers away." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing price skimming with low or competitive pricing. In fact skimming sets a high launch price, above the going rate, for a new product that has no close rival yet: it takes a high margin from the buyers who want to be first, and the price typically comes down later as rivals arrive. Setting the price below established shops to win their customers is penetration pricing; setting it at about the rivals' level is competitive pricing. The test that tells them apart: ask where the launch price sits against the going rate, and whether close rivals already exist. Skimming sits above the going rate and depends on the product being new with no close rival; a low or matching price is aimed at customers that existing rivals already serve. Ondjila has priced below shops that already sell bikes, so it is not skimming. If its electric bike were the first of its kind in town and launched at a high price, the label would fit - for as long as no rival offered the same thing.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact skimming is a high launch price for a new product with no close rival, so a price set below established rivals is penetration (or, at their level, competitive) pricing.

items.prompt: Nderi Phones assembles chargers in Outjo. Its full cost per charger is N$36. Two established rivals sell equivalent chargers in the same shops at N$60. Nderi has a new fabric-cable design no rival yet has; it can make 400 chargers a month at most, and demand at the shops is estimated at 500 a month. Using the figures, consider whether Nderi should launch at N$95 with the new design or at N$55 to match the market.
items.canonical_answer: The figures: launching at N$95 gives a margin of 95 - 36 = 59 per charger, so 400 chargers a month earn 59 x 400 = 23 600, written in Namibian dollars as N$23 600. Launching at N$55 gives 55 - 36 = 19 per charger; if demand ran at the estimated 500 a month the margin would be 19 x 500 = 9 500, that is N$9 500 - but Nderi can make at most 400, so the real ceiling is 19 x 400 = 7 600, that is N$7 600. Judged on capacity the comparison is N$23 600 against N$7 600 a month. Judgement: Nderi should launch at N$95 with the new design. Context: the design is unmatched, the rivals' equivalent sells at N$60, and buyers who want the fabric cable have no rival source while the design lasts - the facts skimming needs. Criterion: what decides it is the capacity limit against the unmatched design - because output is capped at 400, the volume the low price would win cannot be made anyway, so the penetration price would buy demand Nderi cannot fill while giving away margin on every unit it can. Counterargument: the case for N$55 is that penetration wins shelf attention and retailer goodwill, and if the rivals copy the fabric cable, the N$95 skim price loses its footing fast; the alternative also builds a customer base quickly, which matters if the design advantage is short-lived. Condition: the recommendation depends on the design staying unmatched and on the shops actually stocking the higher price - if either fails, the price must fall toward the competitive N$60 level, and the campaign spent teaching buyers a high price would have to be spent again in reverse.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation between the two launch prices. Context: award for using the figures - the margins per charger, the 400 capacity ceiling, the N$23 600 against N$7 600 monthly comparison. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - capacity against the unmatched design. Counterargument: award for the case for N$55 - shelf attention, copied-design risk. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the final recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: price as what the customer pays for one unit, and note that the highest price a product can carry depends on how strongly demand responds - price elastic demand punishes a rise, price inelastic demand absorbs one. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: where demand is price inelastic, a higher price tends to raise revenue because sales barely fall while each remaining sale earns more, so for a needed, rare or habitual product the highest price the market absorbs does serve profit - the view holds there. Paragraph 3, the case against: with price elastic demand, the highest price drives buyers to close substitutes, so revenue falls - and in a market with visible rivals, a business that prices at the ceiling invites entrants into the margin, as the skimming chain shows; also, a price set below cost is not one a business can defend for long, and price far above value breaks the brand's trust with the customers who built it. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view holds only for a product whose demand is price inelastic and whose brand is strong; the criterion is how strongly the quantity demanded responds against the price change, tested by the buyer's alternatives. Recommendation conditional on: the responsiveness of demand staying as assessed, close substitutes staying scarce, and the brand's trust surviving the premium - when any of these conditions changes, the highest carryable price falls with it.

Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - demand's response tested by the buyer's alternatives. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against - elastic demand, rivals and entrants, trust. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - responsiveness, substitutes, brand trust.

items.prompt: Tulela Baskets weaves baskets in a village outside Grootfontein and sells them to two city shops at N$90 each, of which the weavers keep N$50 after transport and the shops' mark-up. A younger weaver wants to open a webshop with photos and a weekly post of new baskets, pricing at N$150 with delivery by courier at N$25 a parcel. The village has patchy network coverage and the collective has no camera. Analyse the situation and recommend what the collective should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the facts split into the opportunity and the threats. The opportunity: selling direct through a webshop keeps the whole price - the customer pays N$150 and no shop takes a mark-up, so the margin per basket rises from N$50 toward 150 - 25 = 125, that is N$125 after courier costs, and the two channels can run side by side, the shops serving buyers who handle baskets before buying. The threats: the buyer cannot touch or try the product before paying, which matters for hand-woven goods, so strong photos and a fair returns promise must do the touching; delivery at N$25 a parcel eats the margin and returns would eat it twice; and the practical gaps are real - patchy network coverage and no camera mean the weekly content the method needs is exactly what the collective cannot yet produce reliably. The brand side: the collective's name and story, told in the posts, is what a webshop sells with - a trusted image lowers the risk an unseen basket carries. Recommendation: trial the webshop small - a smartphone bought once, a posting day each week in Grootfontein where the network holds, prices at N$150 with the courier cost stated, and the two city shops kept on so the collective does not bet its whole income on the trial. Judgement: the trial is worth it because the margin per basket is far higher even after courier costs, and the criterion that decides it is whether the weekly posts can actually be produced and whether buyers who cannot touch the baskets will pay the premium anyway. The judgement is a close one because the infrastructure gaps are the collective's own, so the trial should be sized so its failure costs little and its success can be scaled.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation - the small webshop trial alongside the shops. Context: award for using the facts - the N$50 against N$125 margin comparison, the N$25 courier cost, patchy coverage, no camera, the shops' mark-up. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - producible weekly content and buyers paying unseen. Counterargument: award for the case against - the touch problem, delivery and returns costs, the infrastructure gaps. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on the trial's sizing and the shops being kept.
